'''Trinidadian Creole''' is an [[English-based creole languages|English-based creole language]] commonly spoken throughout the island of [[Trinidad]] in [[Trinidad and Tobago]]. It is distinct from [[Tobagonian Creole]] – particularly at the [[basilectal]] level<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Youssef|James|2004|pp=508, 514}}</ref> – and from other [[Lesser Antilles|Lesser Antillean]] creoles.

English is the country's official language (the national standard variety is [[Trinidadian and Tobagonian English]]), but the main spoken languages are Trinidadian Creole and Tobagonian Creole.<ref>{{cite web |title=What Languages are Spoken in Trinidad and Tobago? |url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/what-languages-are-spoken-in-trinidad-and-tobago.html |website=WorldAtlas |date=August 2017 |access-date=18 May 2025}}</ref> Prior to English being designated as the country’s official language, a French mixed with formerly enslaved  African languages type of Creole was more prominent throughout the island amongst former slaves.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ferreira |first=Jo-Anne S. |title=Trinidad's French Creole Linguistic and Cultural Heritage: Documentation and Revitalisation Issues |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281277304 |website=ResearchGate |date=June 2015 |access-date=18 May 2025}}</ref> 

English became the country's official language in 1823. Consequently, government and educational institutions endorsement of the language change significantly and influenced the progressive transition and phaseout of the former French mixed Creole to an English based Creole, that is now more widely spoken.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ferreira |first=Jo-Anne S. |title=Trinidad's French Creole Linguistic and Cultural Heritage: Documentation and Revitalisation Issues |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281277304 |website=ResearchGate |date=June 2015 |access-date=18 May 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=APiCS Online - Survey chapter: Trinidad English Creole |url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/6 |access-date=2022-03-13 |website=apics-online.info}}</ref> 

Both creoles contain elements from a variety of other languages, brought to the island over time by mostly African slaves and East Indian settlers. As of 2011, there were 1 million native speakers.<ref>{{cite web |title=Trinidad Language: Exploring the World of Trinidadian Creole |url=https://davidsbeenhere.com/2023/08/12/trinidad-language-exploring-the-world-of-trinidadian-creole/ |website=David's Been Here |date=12 August 2023 |access-date=18 May 2025}}</ref>

== History ==
Like other [[Caribbean]] English-based creoles, Trinidadian Creole English has a primarily English-derived vocabulary. In the mid-nineteenth century, when the use of slavery was demolished, people from China, Portuguese islands, Venezuela, Madeira, India, west Africa, Syria and Lebanon were used as labourers for the island.<ref name=":1" /> The island also has a creole with a largely [[French language|French]] lexicon, which was in widespread use until the late nineteenth century, when it started to be gradually replaced, due to influence and pressure from the British.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Youssef|James|2004|pp=510–511}}</ref>

[[Arawakan languages|Arawak]], [[Bhojpuri language|Bhojpuri]], [[Carib language|Carib]], [[Antillean Creole|French Creole (Patois)]], [[Spanish language|Spanish]] and [[Niger–Congo languages|West African languages]] have also influenced the language, to varying degrees.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/6 | title=Trinidad English Creole | publisher=Apics-Online.info | accessdate=2025-04-22}}</ref> In addition, Trinidadian linguist Jo-Anne Ferreira sees occasional words influenced by [[Arabic language|Arabic]] and [[Chinese language|Chinese]].<ref>Jo-Anne Sharon Ferreira. [https://web.archive.org/web/20110724162817/http://vsites.unb.br/il/liv/crioul/textos/ferreira.htm (A Brief Overview of) The Sociolinguistic History of Trinidad & Tobago]. University of the West Indies. unb.br</ref>

==Phonological features==
Although there is considerable variation, some generalizations can be made about the speech of Trinidad:
* Like a number of related creoles, Trinidadian English Creole is [[Rhoticity in English|non-rhotic]], meaning that {{IPA|/r/}} does not occur after vowels, except in recent [[loanword]]s or names from Spanish, Hindi/Bhojpuri, and Arabic.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Amastae|1979|p=191}}</ref>
* In mesolectal forms, ''cut'', ''cot'', ''caught'', and ''curt'' are all pronounced with {{IPA|[ɒ]}}.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Youssef|James|2004|p=516}}</ref>
* The [[dental fricative]]s of English are replaced with [[dental stop|dental]]/[[alveolar stop]]s.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Youssef|James|2004|p=517}}</ref>
* Trinidad English Creole is usually syllable-timed and not stress-timed; therefore it often has full vowels where Standard English has the reduced form /ə/. [https://apics-online.info/surveys/6]
* Although, there is no clear connection between pitch and stress,<ref>{{Cite web |title=APiCS Online - Survey chapter: Trinidad English Creole |url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/6 |access-date=2022-03-13 |website=apics-online.info}}</ref> words of Trinidad English Creole are marked by a stress-initial syllable.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Lindsay Nurse |first=Keisha T. |last2=Martinez |first2=Silvia |last3=Franklin |first3=Amber |last4=Ferreira |first4=Jo-Anne S. |last5=Lucker |first5=Jay |last6=Wallace |first6=Gloriajean |date=April 2025 |title=Culturally and Linguistically Responsive Speech Sound Assessment Considerations for Speakers of Trinidadian English and Trinidadian English Creole |url=https://pubs.asha.org/doi/10.1044/2024_PERSP-24-00074 |journal=Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups |language=en |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=595–607 |doi=10.1044/2024_PERSP-24-00074 |issn=2381-4764|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Morphological features ==

* Trinidad English Creole verbs do not use marks for people or numbers {-ed}, {-s}.<ref name=":0" />

==Usage==
Both Trinidad and Tobago<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Minderhout|1977|pp=168–169}}</ref> feature [[post-creole speech continuum|creole continua]] between more conservative Creole forms and forms much closer to [[Trinidadian English]], with the former being more common in spontaneous speech and the latter in more formal speech.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Winford|1985|pp=352–353}}</ref> Trinidad English Creole is one of the first languages learnt for most speakers. Trinidadian English is introduced in primary schools which are carried out in standardized English.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=Guyanne |date=2020 |title=Variability and acceptability in Trinidadian English |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/weng.12485 |journal=World Englishes |language=en |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=462–479 |doi=10.1111/weng.12485 |issn=0883-2919|doi-access=free }}</ref> Because of the social values attributed to linguistic forms, the more common varieties (that is, more creolized forms) carry little prestige in certain contexts.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Winford|1985|p=353}}</ref>

== Example words and phrases ==
*{{lang|trf|back chat}}: insolence<ref name=tobagowi>[http://www.tobagowi.com/culture/dictionAF.htm tobagowi.com] dictionary of  terms for Trinidad and Tobago</ref>
*''bacchanal'': any incident or time marked by drama, scandal, confusion or conflict<ref>{{Cite web |title=bacchanal at Wiwords.com |url=http://wiwords.com/word/bacchanal |access-date=2022-03-13 |website=wiwords.com |language=en}}</ref>
*''bad-john'': a bully or gangster.<ref name=tobagowi/><ref>Kirt Morris, [https://triniinxisle.com/2018/09/09/trinidad-slangs-badjohn/ "Trini Phrase: Bad John"], TriniInXisle.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=UK English Dictionary |url=https://www.lexico.com/definition/bad-john |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210821013727/https://www.lexico.com/definition/bad-john |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 21, 2021 |website=Lexico.com |publisher=Dictionary.com/Oxford University Press |access-date=21 August 2021}}</ref>
*''bazoodee'': light-headed, in shock, or crazy.
*''bhowgie/bhauji'': Indian sister-in-law (brother's wife), but is also used to address any slightly older [[Indo-Trinidadian]] woman than oneself.
*''bobolee'': someone easily taken advantage of; also used to refer to an effigy made on [[Good Friday]] that is beaten and used to represent [[Judas]] and traitors.
*''broughtupsy/brought-upsie'': good manners, proper upbringing or home training.<ref>{{Cite web |title=broughtupsy at Wiwords.com |url=http://wiwords.com/word/broughtupsy |access-date=2022-03-13 |website=wiwords.com |language=en}}</ref>
*''buss-up shut'': another name for [[Paratha]] from its resemblance to a bursted shirt when the paratha is clapped after cooking.
*''[[calypso music|calypso]]'': a musical or lyrical comment on something, particularly popular during Carnival.<ref name=tobagowi/>
*''chamkay'': to dance and shake the waist originally meant to shine
*''chinksin'': miserly; distributing less than one could or should.<ref name=WiWords>[http://www.wiwords.com/browse/Trinidad+and+Tobago/all WiWords.com] dictionary of the West Indies</ref>
*''[[Churel|churile]]'': a wretched women; also a ghost of a pregnant women in local folklore.
*''comess'': drama and confusion.
*''cunumunu'': awkward or idiot.
*''daru'': rum
*''dingolay'': cheerful dance that involves fast paced movements.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Caribbean Dictionary|url=http://wiwords.com/|access-date=2021-08-20|website=Wiwords|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=dingolay - Wiktionary|url=https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/dingolay|access-date=2021-08-20|website=en.wiktionary.org|language=en}}</ref>
*''dotish'': stupid or incompetent.
*''[[Dougla]]'': a person having both Indian and African parentage.<ref name=tobagowi/>
*''doux-doux/doo-doo'': sweetheart or darling.
*''[[Fête|fête]]'': party
*''[[ganja]]'': [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]]
*''goat-mouth'': to have or give bad luck with one's words.
*''[[Girmitiyas|jahaji]]'': the literal meaning is "of the ship"; used to refer to the Indian [[Indian indenture system|indentured laborers]].
*''jhanjat'': confusion<ref>https://www.facebook.com/story.php?story_fbid=3995250657158295&id=100063788252487</ref>
*''[[Jumbee|jumbee]]'': a ghost or demonic spirit.
*''junjunnee'': cramp
*''korhee'': lazy
*''kuchur'': trouble
*''labar-labar/lab-lab'': to do carelessly.
*''lime/limming'': to relax and hangout.
*''[[Madrasi|Madrassi]]'': a person with [[South India]]n heritage.
*''macco'': someone who gets into other people's business.<ref name=tobagowi/>
*''maljo/mal yeaux'': a sickness manifested upon newborn babies and young animals (like puppies) out of envy or ill wishes.<ref name=WiWords/>
*''mamaguy'': to deceive or mislead by flattery.
*''mamoo'': Indian maternal uncle; also used to refer to any older [[Indo-Trinidadian]] man.
*''najar'': [[Evil eye|evil eye]]
*''nara'': abdominal pain
* ''neemakharam'': ingrate
* ''ole' talk/old talk'': superficial chatting
*''pothound'': a mongrel dog of no specific breed or whose breed is unknown; mutt.<ref name=WiWords/>
* ''poohar'': sloppy or untidy.<ref>{{cite web | title=A poohar state of emergency | date=7 January 2025 | url=https://trinidadexpress.com/opinion/columnists/a-poohar-state-of-emergency/article_f291e280-cd5e-11ef-bfc2-376884625397.html }}</ref>
*''quelbe/quelba/quilbay'': a kind of African dance possibly of Congo origin, comprising songs, drumming and dances performed by women. 
*''rachifee/ratcheefi/ratchifi/rachify'': something done in a makeshift, careless, or slightly devious way.
*''tabanca'': heartbreak<ref name=tobagowi/>
*''tanty/tantie'': aunt
*''[[Tarkari|tarkari/talkari]]'': any vegetarian [[curry]] dish.
*''toting feelings'': not able to move on from a previous relationship.
*''ups kabat'': a type of game played with marbles, otherwise known as "marble pitch".<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Winer|Boos|1993|p=46}}</ref>
*''Venee'': [[Venezuelans|Venezuelan]]
*''wajang'': someone with bad conduct or unworthy.
*''whine'': a dance involving gyrating of the hips.
*''zaboca'': avocado<ref>{{Cite web|title=zaboca at Wiwords.com|url=http://wiwords.com/word/zaboca|access-date=2021-08-20|website=wiwords.com|language=en}}</ref>
